title: Homeschool days or hours: check what applies
dek: Check whether your homeschool route requires days, hours or both, then build a record that shows the right measure for each child.
metaDescription: Check whether your homeschool route requires days, hours or both, then build a record that shows the right measure for each child.

paragraphs: You may need to count homeschool days, hours, either one, or a combination. The answer comes from the rules for your state and education route, not from a national school-year number. Finding no result in a search means the question is unresolved, not that you are exempt.

A parent can keep a beautifully detailed hourly log and still miss a required day count. Another can spend evenings timing lessons their route does not require them to time. Before choosing a tracker, establish which measure matters and what evidence must accompany it. This is a US verification method, not a legal opinion about your family.

body.heading: Different rules produce different records
rows: Pennsylvania home education: 180 days OR 900 elementary/990 secondary hours.
Select the permitted measure and document it consistently.
Colorado nonpublic home-based program: at least 172 days averaging four instructional contact hours daily.
A tick for each date alone does not show the whole requirement.
You cannot locate the applicable instructional-time provision.
Ask the responsible authority; do not record no requirement as a conclusion.

body.heading: Read the small connecting words
paragraphs: In the [Pennsylvania guide](https://www.pa.gov/content/dam/copapwp-pagov/en/education/documents/instruction/home-education-and-private-tutoring/home%20education%20and%20private%20tutoring%20guide.pdf), the alternatives are connected by "or." In the [Colorado law](https://www.cde.state.co.us/node/773), instructional days are combined with an average contact-hours condition. Turning either into a generic 180-day calendar loses information. These examples apply only to their described programs.

Check the age or grade range, school-year definition, part-year entry provisions and whether prior school attendance can be included. Do not automatically prorate a full-year figure when you withdraw midyear. Ask how the rule applies and retain the answer. Testing, subjects, portfolios and notice requirements remain separate questions.

body.heading: Establish your counting rule
items: Identify the state, legal route and each child's relevant age or grade. Do not assume siblings necessarily have identical duties.
Find the official instructional-time or attendance section. Search the law linked by the agency as well as its overview page.
Write the exact measure: days, hours, either, or combined. Include any minimum, average or definition the rule uses.
Confirm what activities may count, how shared teaching is recorded and whether travel, independent work or outside classes need additional evidence.
Find out whether the record is retained, submitted or reviewed and by whom. A required count is not necessarily a required monthly filing.
Keep the rule, URL, checked date and any written clarification beside the log. Review after a move or change of route.

body.heading: Example: why the same calendar can mislead
paragraphs: Invented example: Avery marks 172 dates on a calendar and assumes the number alone proves compliance. On rereading the applicable Colorado provision, Avery sees the average instructional contact-hours condition. The family keeps the date record but adds actual qualifying time and activity notes, then asks the responsible office how to handle a previously incomplete period.

The correction is not to manufacture four hours on every old date. It is to distinguish existing evidence, reasonably reconstructed information and unknown time. A log that identifies its limits is more useful than a total no one can explain. If a submission is already due, ask for help with that situation before spending days redesigning the log.

body.heading: Keep the entry small but attributable
rows: Who participated and the actual date.
Subject or activity and enough detail to identify the work.
The qualifying day marker or actual time, as applicable.
Work sample reference, outside class record, or a labelled reconstruction.

body.heading: Count actual participation, not planned lessons
paragraphs: Use your schedule to plan and your log to record what happened. A canceled class does not become completed instruction because it remained on the calendar. For a shared field trip, identify each participating child rather than adding the outing to a household total that cannot be separated later.

An hour cannot be counted twice for the same child merely because an activity touches two subjects. How an interdisciplinary activity is categorized and what time qualifies are questions for the applicable rules. Keep your description factual rather than adjusting it to reach a target. For an ongoing routine, [homeschool attendance records](/guides/homeschool-attendance-what-to-track) addresses the day-to-day record.

body.heading: When to stop guessing
paragraphs: Ask for written clarification if an agency overview conflicts with the statute, your child begins midyear, you are switching routes, or an evaluator requests something you cannot trace to the applicable requirements. Where legal compliance or a truancy concern is at stake, contact qualified state-specific help.

A voluntary count can still help you plan when no count applies. Label it as your planning tool rather than a compliance measure. Do not turn a private target into a claim that you have met every education duty. Record quality and educational progress are related to, but not the same as, time totals.

items.q: Does a homeschool day have to last a set number of hours?
items.a: That depends on the applicable rule. A day-count requirement may have a duration condition, an averaging condition, or no separately stated hourly measure. Colorado is one example combining days and average contact hours. Read the actual definition rather than assuming that any short activity creates a qualifying school day.

items.q: Can I choose hours instead of days?
items.a: Only if your route permits that alternative. Pennsylvania home education provides an either-or example, but it does not establish a choice elsewhere. Record which option you are using and what evidence supports it. Do not switch measures simply to make an incomplete record appear to reach a target.

items.q: What if I did not track time from the start?
items.a: Keep the records you do have, such as dated work, calendars and class confirmations. Label reconstructed entries and uncertainty rather than inventing precision. Ask the responsible authority or a qualified adviser how to address a missing required record, especially if a filing or review deadline is close.
